title: Silicon Quantum Computing Traces 25-Year Roadmap to Atomic-Precision Manufacturing in Nature Nanotechnology - Quantum Computing Report
gist: In a Nature Nanotechnology Comment, Silicon Quantum Computing's Ludwik Kranz and Michelle Simmons describe 25 years of phosphorus-in-silicon progress, now an automated STM lithography process with 0.13 nm placement accuracy, 99.99%+ single-qubit fidelity, and early commercial analog simulators. They say universal fault tolerance now depends on 3D integration with foundry-built control electronics.

insights.claim: According to SQC's Nature Nanotechnology Comment, scanning tunneling microscope hydrogen lithography has moved from a manual research tool to an automated industrial process placing phosphorus atoms with 0.13 nm spatial accuracy at rates exceeding hundreds of thousands of qubit registers per day.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Throughput claims, if they hold, answer the main objection to atom-by-atom fabrication, namely that it cannot scale.

insights.claim: The platform relies on high-purity isotopically purified silicon (28Si) and epitaxial encapsulation, achieving single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.99% and coherence times beyond 30 seconds.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Materials purity is the source of the coherence advantage and is the moat to watch.

insights.claim: The authors describe the phosphorus-in-silicon '14/15 platform' as having progressed over 25 years from Kane's proposal and STM single-atom placement (1998-2000s) through single-atom transistors and 30-second nuclear spin coherence (2010s) to multi-qubit processors (2020s).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A long, stepwise development arc suggests incremental de-risking rather than a sudden breakthrough.

insights.claim: In the 2020s phase SQC reports record-low 1/f charge noise in epitaxial devices, fast two-qubit exchange logic, and an 11-qubit multi-register processor, with two-qubit gate fidelities above 99.9% and multi-qubit algorithms run above fault-tolerance thresholds.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Fidelity above 99.9% is notable, but 11 qubits is far from utility scale; the scaling path is the open question.
insights.locator: Historical evolution table, Multi-Qubit Scaling row

themes.theme: Commercial analog products without full error correction

insights.claim: The present industrial phase includes 15,000 quantum dot analog simulators and Fermi-Hubbard 2D atom array simulations, deployed as commercial analog simulators and quantum feature generators into classical HPC and AI pipelines without requiring full quantum error correction.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Near-term revenue from analog simulation integrated with HPC and AI workflows is a path to monetize before fault tolerance arrives.
insights.locator: Historical evolution table, Industrial Integration row

insights.claim: The authors say the remaining route to universal fault tolerance centers on industrial-scale 3D integration with foundry-built classical control electronics and cryogenic interconnects.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Dependence on semiconductor foundry integration ties this modality's timeline to foundry partnerships and packaging progress.

insights.claim: Because electron wavefunctions in silicon extend only a few nanometers, the platform has higher thermal headroom than superconducting circuits, allowing utility-scale processors with hundreds of thousands of physical qubits to operate within a single dilution refrigerator.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: If true, wiring and cooling overhead per qubit is lower than for superconducting rivals; this is a claim by SQC's own leadership and not independently validated in the article.
